summary: Westchester County's 1926 steel fire tower on Cross River Mountain was taken down around 1980 to 1982; a restoration is being built on the summit and is not yet open.

facts.design: Steel fire observation tower of the standard State Conservation Commission type; 1926 notices give 60 or 69 feet tall
facts.status_note: The original tower was taken down around 1980 to 1982; a restoration is being assembled on the summit in 2026 and is not yet open
facts.agency: Westchester County Parks, Recreation, and Conservation

access.note: The restored tower is still under construction and not yet officially open (project update, September 2026)

events.note: Erected by the Westchester County Park Commission on Stony Ridge, inside Ward Pound Ridge Reservation
Observer on part-time duty from September, watching all day from October
Nine fires broke out in the region in 1931; all were put out before serious damage
Notice says the State Department would continue operating the tower
About 500 fires reported from the tower between 1966 and 1968, per a 1975 county report quoted by the register
Register's summary line says taken down in 1980; its description says around 1982
Register's description says taken down without county approval around 1982
County Board of Supervisors approved funding to return a fire tower to the summit
Base section anchored to foundations in November 2025; restoration under way
Restoration sections assembled through August and September; tower not yet open

evidence.supports: tower erected in 1926 and used by the community until the 1970s
evidence.quote: The beautiful and historic fire tower was erected in 1926 and was used by the community until the 1970’s.

evidence.supports: Stony Ridge chosen by Westchester County Park Commission as site of fire observation tower, 1926, about 860 feet
evidence.quote: Stony Ridge, the highest point in the Poundridge Reservation, having an elevation of about 860 feet, has been chosen by the Westchester County Park Commission as the site of a fire observation tower.

evidence.supports: steel of the standard State Conservation Commission type already transported to the site
evidence.quote: The steel work for the tower, of the standard type used by the State Conservation Commission, has already been transported to the site of the tower.

evidence.supports: planned height 60 feet, observer enclosure about 920 feet
evidence.quote: The tower itself will have a height of 60 feet, so that the observer's enclosure at the top will have an elevation of about 920 feet.

evidence.supports: another 1926 notice gives planned height 69 feet
evidence.quote: The tower itself will have a height of 69 feet so that the observer's enclosure at the top will be at an elevation of about 920 feet.

evidence.supports: observer to be stationed from November 1 until first real snowfall
evidence.quote: It is expected that the fire observer will be stationed there from November 1 until the first real snowfall.

evidence.supports: planned telephone connection to Park Commission headquarters
evidence.quote: The observation post will have a telephone connection to the Park Commission's headquarters at the reservation

evidence.supports: 1929 notice calls the summit Stone Hill
evidence.quote: The tower is 60 feet high and located at the highest point of the reservation at the top of Stone Hill.

evidence.supports: 1932 notice calls the summit Stone Mountain and says the lookout was built in 1926
evidence.quote: The lookout station was built in 1926 on top of Stone Mountain, the highest point in the reservation, and commands a view of the country for miles around.

evidence.supports: observer watching all day since October 1929
evidence.quote: Since October the observer has kept watch in the tower all day.

evidence.supports: State Department to continue operating the tower (1932)
evidence.quote: It was learned this week that the State Department will continue its operation of the Cross River Fire tower

evidence.supports: nine fires in 1931, all put out before serious damage
evidence.quote: Nine fires broke out in the region during 1931, eight of them in farm lands adjacent to the reservation, and all were put out before any serious damage had been done.

evidence.supports: County Parks operated until the 1930s, then NYS Conservation Department
evidence.quote: The County Parks operated the tower until the 1930’s when the NYS Conservation Department began its operations.

evidence.supports: about 500 fires reported from the tower, 1966 to 1968, per 1975 county report
evidence.quote: According to a Westchester County government report from 1975 indicates that about 500 fires were reported from the tower between 1966 and 1968, with tower observers working with aerial support to pinpoint their locations.

evidence.supports: DEC decommissioned the tower in 1971; taken down around 1982 without county approval
evidence.quote: The tower was decommissioned by the DEC in 1971 and was taken down without county approval around 1982.

evidence.supports: register summary line gives taken down 1980
evidence.quote: Original 1926, taken down 1980, restoration in 2026.

evidence.supports: register gives summit height of 960 feet
evidence.quote: The tower stood a staggering 960 feet above sea level.

evidence.supports: original stood at highest point of Cross River Mountain
evidence.quote: The tower stood at the highest point of Cross River Mountain.

evidence.supports: original had a 360 degree view with visibility of 50 to 100 miles
evidence.quote: It had a spectacular 360 degree view with a visibility of 50-100 miles depending on the weather.

evidence.supports: registered May 27, 2026
Friends of the Fire Tower 501(c)(3) raising money through races and donations
evidence.quote: Through the Fire Tower Trail Half Marathon & 10k in June we raised over $1,500 in three months from supporters via the Friends of the Fire Tower 501c3.

evidence.supports: county Board of Supervisors approved funding to return a tower to the summit
evidence.quote: Board of Supervisors has approved funding to return a fire tower to the the summit.

evidence.supports: section 2 lifted atop section 1, base anchored to foundations since November 2025
evidence.quote: Most recently, section 2 was moved up via crane atop section 1 (the base, which has been anchored to the foundations since November 2025).

evidence.supports: structure about 40 feet high by mid-August 2026
evidence.quote: This structure is now approximately 40′ high.

evidence.supports: section 3 still being assembled on September 6, 2026

corrections.why: The project says the tower is not yet officially open, and no source read says the tower can be entered by permission

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The register gives 1980 in its summary line and around 1982 in its description, with no other source read dating the removal. Left unresolved in the story.
1926 notices give the planned tower as 60 feet in one and 69 feet in another; the register gives 870 ft (265 m) for the site and 960 feet in its description. Left unresolved in the story.
Newspaper notices call the summit Stony Ridge (1926), Stone Hill (1929) and Stone Mountain (1932).

notes_for_editor: The original tower is gone; the brief's status 'gone' is right, but a restoration (described by the register and project as a restoration, with steel sections going up in 2026) is under construction and not open, so access is set to closed and the brief's 'permission' is proposed as a correction. Removal date conflicts inside the register (1980 vs around 1982) and the elevation/height figures disagree across sources; both are left open in the story. The 2023 board-funding line is a single newsletter item; the county's own record was not read. No photos found; a future check of crmfiretower.org after the tower opens should confirm access and any visitor rules. Used 0 WebSearch calls and about 8 page reads.
